title: Independent events
summary: Two events are independent when the probability of both equals the product of the probabilities. Pairwise independence does not give the triple product.
intuition:
Independence is a statement about a product. Events $A$ and $B$ are independent when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Knowing that $B$ occurred does not change the probability of $A$: if $P(B)>0$, the product rule is exactly $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$. The definition does not mention disjointness. Disjointness is $P(A\cap B)=0$, which is a different equation.

For three events, pairwise independence is the three equations for the pairs. Mutual independence asks for those three equations and one more, $P(A\cap B\cap C)=P(A)P(B)P(C)$. The extra equation is not free. There is a four-outcome sample space, written out below, in which every pair multiplies correctly and the triple does not. Pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence.

The product extends to complements. If $A$ and $B$ are independent, then so are $A$ and $B^c$, because $P(A\cap B^c)=P(A)-P(A)P(B)=P(A)P(B^c)$. For a mutually independent family the same idea gives the probability that none of the events occur: multiply the complementary probabilities. That step is illegal if you only checked the pairs.

definitions.body: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. If $P(B)>0$, this is equivalent to $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$.
A family of events is pairwise independent when every pair of distinct events is independent. For three events, that is three product equations and no claim about the triple intersection.
Events $A$, $B$, and $C$ are mutually independent when they are pairwise independent and also $P(A\cap B\cap C)=P(A)P(B)P(C)$. For a larger family, every finite subcollection must multiply.

formulas.name: Two-event product
formulas.note: This is the definition of independence. It is not the same statement as $P(A\cap B)=0$.

formulas.name: Triple product
formulas.note: Required for mutual independence, in addition to the three pairwise products.

formulas.name: Complement stays independent
formulas.note: True whenever $A$ and $B$ are independent. The proof is $P(A)-P(A\cap B)=P(A)(1-P(B))$.

properties: If $P(A)>0$ and $P(B)>0$, then $A$ and $B$ cannot be both independent and mutually exclusive. The product $P(A)P(B)$ would be positive, while mutual exclusion forces the intersection probability to be 0.
Pairwise independence of three events does not imply $P(A\cap B\cap C)=P(A)P(B)P(C)$.
The certain event $S$ is independent of every event, because $P(A\cap S)=P(A)=P(A)P(S)$.
If $A$, $B$, and $C$ are mutually independent, then $P(A^c\cap B^c\cap C^c)=P(A^c)P(B^c)P(C^c)$.
Independence is a property of the probability measure, not of the shapes of the sets. Disjoint sets are dependent whenever both have positive probability.

examples.title: Two dice, two events on different dice
examples.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled, and the 36 ordered outcomes are equally likely. Let $A$ be the event that the first die is even, and let $B$ be the event that the second die shows 1 or 2. Are $A$ and $B$ independent?
steps: The first die is even on 3 of 6 faces, and the second die is free, so $P(A)=18/36=1/2$. The second die shows 1 or 2 on 2 of 6 faces, so $P(B)=12/36=1/3$.
The intersection needs the first die even and the second die in $\{1,2\}$: $3\times 2=6$ outcomes, so $P(A\cap B)=6/36=1/6$.
The product is $P(A)P(B)=(1/2)(1/3)=1/6$, which equals the intersection probability. The events are independent.

examples.title: Four outcomes: pairwise, but not mutual
examples.prompt: The sample space is $\{a,b,c,d\}$, with each outcome of probability $1/4$. Let $A=\{a,b\}$, $B=\{a,c\}$, and $C=\{a,d\}$. Check pairwise independence and mutual independence.
steps: Each of $A$, $B$, and $C$ contains two outcomes, so $P(A)=P(B)=P(C)=1/2$.
Each pairwise intersection is the singleton $\{a\}$, with probability $1/4$. The product of any two probabilities is $(1/2)(1/2)=1/4$. All three pairs are independent.
The triple intersection is also $\{a\}$, so $P(A\cap B\cap C)=1/4$. The product of the three probabilities is $(1/2)^3=1/8$. Because $1/4\neq 1/8$, the three events are not mutually independent.
examples.answer: The events are pairwise independent, and they are not mutually independent, because $P(A\cap B\cap C)=1/4$ while $P(A)P(B)P(C)=1/8$.

traps: Reading $P(A\cap B)=0$ as independence. That equation is mutual exclusion. Positive mutually exclusive events are dependent.
Checking only the three pairs and then multiplying three probabilities. Pairwise independence does not give $P(A\cap B\cap C)=P(A)P(B)P(C)$, as the four-outcome example shows.
Replacing the definition by $P(A\mid B)=P(B)$. Independence says $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ when $P(B)>0$, not $P(A\mid B)=P(B)$.
Cancelling a zero-probability event. If $P(B)=0$, the conditional probability $P(A\mid B)$ is undefined, so the conditional form of the test cannot be used.
python:
from fractions import Fraction
assert Fraction(1, 2) * Fraction(1, 3) == Fraction(6, 36)
assert Fraction(1, 4) == Fraction(1, 2) * Fraction(1, 2)
assert Fraction(1, 4) != Fraction(1, 8)
none = Fraction(1, 3) * Fraction(1, 4) * Fraction(3, 5)
assert 1 - none == Fraction(19, 20)
union = Fraction(1, 5) + Fraction(2, 5) - Fraction(2, 25)
assert union == Fraction(13, 25)
print(float(Fraction(19, 20)), float(union))

questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A)=2/5$ and $P(B)=1/4$. Then $P(A\cap B)$ equals
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $1/10$.

Independence gives the product $(2/5)(1/4)=2/20=1/10$. Option B is the union $2/5+1/4-1/10=13/20$, which is a different event. Option C would be the intersection only if the events were mutually exclusive.

questions.stem: Events $A$ and $B$ are independent, with $P(A)=2/5$ and $P(B)=1/2$. Then $P(A\cup B)$ equals
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $7/10$.

The intersection is $(2/5)(1/2)=1/5$. Inclusion-exclusion then gives $2/5+1/2-1/5=4/10+5/10-2/10=7/10$. Option B adds the two probabilities and does not subtract the intersection.

questions.stem: A sample space has four equally likely outcomes $\{a,b,c,d\}$. Let $A=\{a,b\}$, $B=\{a,c\}$, and $C=\{a,d\}$. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

Each single event has probability $1/2$, and each pairwise intersection is $\{a\}$ with probability $1/4=(1/2)(1/2)$. The triple intersection is also $\{a\}$, so its probability is $1/4$, while $(1/2)^3=1/8$. D is false, and the family is pairwise independent without being mutually independent.

questions.stem: Events $A$, $B$, and $C$ are mutually independent, with $P(A)=2/3$, $P(B)=3/4$, and $P(C)=2/5$. Let $p$ be the probability that at least one of the three events occurs. Enter $20p$.
questions.solution:
The answer is **19**.

Mutual independence passes to the complements, so the probability that none occur is $(1/3)(1/4)(3/5)=1/20$. Therefore $p=1-1/20=19/20$, and $20p=19$. Multiplying only the pairwise pieces would not justify this step.
